Cava Guide

Spain’s celebrated sparkling wine: fine bubbles, crisp acidity and elegant flavours.

By Nigel A. Thomas, Hospitality Executive · Updated October 2026

Few sparkling wines offer as much pleasure for the price as Cava. It has the fine bubbles, the crisp freshness and the celebratory feel of the world’s great sparkling wines, yet it is made in Spain, priced for everyday enjoyment and flexible enough to move from a breakfast mimosa to a late-night tapas table. For hotels, restaurants, bars and banquet operations, Cava is one of the most useful bottles you can stock: it suits brunch, aperitifs, receptions, toasts and cocktails, and it gives guests a premium experience without a premium price tag.

This guide goes with the Day 17 Cava poster below. It follows the same path: what Cava is, how it is made, the grapes behind it, the sweetness levels, the foods it loves, the cocktails it anchors, and how to serve and sell it with confidence. After more than thirty years in hospitality, on ships, in hotels and in restaurants across India, the Middle East and the USA, I have found that guests respond best to clear, honest, enthusiastic recommendations. The knowledge below gives you exactly that.

What Is Cava?

Cava is a Spanish sparkling wine made using the traditional method, known in French as Méthode Traditionnelle, in which the wine undergoes a second fermentation inside the bottle. It comes mainly from the Penedès region in Catalonia, in north-eastern Spain, with the town of Sant Sadurní d’Anoia widely regarded as its capital. It is known for its fine bubbles, freshness, crisp acidity and elegant flavours.

The name comes from the Catalan word for cave or cellar, a reference to the underground cellars where the bottles age. Cava is protected by its own appellation, the Cava DO (Denominación de Origen), which sets rules on where the wine can be made, which grapes may be used, how long it must age and how it must be labelled. Although most Cava is produced in Catalonia, the appellation also covers several other Spanish regions. Cava can be made in different styles, from very dry to sweeter, in white and rosé, and occasionally in vintage expressions.

A Short History of Cava

The story of Cava is usually traced to 1872, when Josep Raventós of the Codorníu house in Sant Sadurní d’Anoia produced the first bottle-fermented sparkling wine in Catalonia, inspired by the methods used in Champagne. For many years these wines were sold in Spain under French-style names. The word Cava was adopted in the 1970s, and the Cava DO was formalised in 1986, giving the wine its own identity and set of rules. Today it is one of Spain’s most important wine exports and is enjoyed in markets around the world. Knowing this short story is useful on the floor, because guests enjoy a good origin story as much as a good glass.

The Traditional Method: How Cava Gets Its Bubbles

The traditional method is the same technique used for Champagne, and it is the reason Cava’s bubbles are fine and persistent. The poster highlights it with the words “second fermentation in bottle”. Here is how it works:

  • 1. The base wine. Grapes are harvested early to retain acidity and are pressed gently. The juice ferments into a dry, high-acid still wine, and different grape varieties and vineyards are often blended.
  • 2. Tirage. The blended base wine is bottled with a small amount of yeast and sugar, called the liqueur de tirage, and the bottle is sealed.
  • 3. Second fermentation. Inside the sealed bottle, the yeast consumes the sugar, producing a little extra alcohol and carbon dioxide. Because the gas cannot escape, it dissolves into the wine and creates the bubbles.
  • 4. Ageing on the lees. The spent yeast cells, called lees, remain in the bottle. As they break down slowly, they add complexity, a creamy texture and toasty, bready flavours. The longer the contact, the more these notes develop.
  • 5. Riddling. The bottles are gradually tilted and turned so that the sediment collects in the neck, traditionally by hand on racks and now often by machine.
  • 6. Disgorgement. The neck is frozen and the temporary cap is removed. The pressure pushes the plug of sediment out, leaving a clear wine.
  • 7. Dosage. A small amount of wine and sugar, the liqueur d’expédition, is added to set the final sweetness level, and the bottle is sealed with its cork and wire cage.

Cava must complete this second fermentation in the bottle in which it is sold, and the minimum pressure is set by regulation. This is what separates it from cheaper sparkling wines made by faster tank methods.

In short, Cava offers bottle-fermented quality at a friendly price, with a flavour profile all its own. If you want to learn more about the wine regions of the country that inspired its method, our guide to the wine regions of France covers Champagne’s homeland.

Key Grape Varieties

Traditional Cava is built on three native Spanish white grapes, with several additional varieties permitted. Understanding what each contributes helps you explain the wine in simple words.

Macabeo (Viura)

Macabeo, known as Viura in Rioja, gives freshness, floral aromas and elegance. It is the most widely planted of the three and provides a light, fruity backbone to many blends.

Xarel·lo

Xarel·lo adds structure, acidity and ageing potential. It is the most characterful Cava grape, with a rich, earthy, citrus-peel quality, and it is the key to the longer-aged wines.

Parellada

Parellada provides finesse, freshness and delicate aromas. It is typically grown at higher, cooler elevations and contributes lightness and a floral, apple-like character.

Also permitted: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir

Chardonnay is a permitted white variety that adds complexity and body, and many producers use it to give extra richness to the blend. Pinot Noir is a permitted red variety that is used for rosé Cava. Other authorised red varieties may also be used for rosé.

Ageing Categories: Why Time Matters

The length of time a Cava rests on its lees shapes its flavour and often its price. Under the current rules, the main tiers are:

  • Cava de Guarda: the standard tier, aged for a minimum of nine months. Fresh, fruity and approachable.
  • Reserva: aged for at least 18 months, with more toasty, creamy character.
  • Gran Reserva: aged for at least 30 months, with greater depth, complexity and finesse. These are Brut Nature, Extra Brut or Brut in style.
  • Cava de Paraje Calificado: the top tier, from a single, qualified vineyard site, aged for at least 36 months.

Regulations evolve, so check the current rules or the producer’s technical sheet when you need precise information for a menu or wine list.

Sweetness Levels of Cava

Sweetness is the single most useful thing to understand on a Cava label, because it determines both the taste and the pairing. It is measured as residual sugar in grams per litre (g/L) and is set at the dosage stage. The poster shows the main levels:

StyleResidual sugarCharacter
Brut Nature0 to 3 g/LNo added sugar after second fermentation. Very dry with a pure, crisp taste.
Extra Brut0 to 6 g/LVery dry, fresh and crisp.
Brut0 to 12 g/LThe most common style. Balanced and versatile.
Seco12 to 32 g/LSlightly dry to off-dry, a little sweeter.
Semi-Seco32 to 50 g/LNoticeably sweeter, fruity and smooth.

A small technical note: in the official categories the 12 to 32 g/L band is divided into Extra Seco (12 to 17 g/L) and Seco (17 to 32 g/L), and wines above 50 g/L are labelled Dulce. The poster groups the middle band together for simplicity. For most guests, Brut is the safe, popular choice. Brut Nature and Extra Brut suit those who like very dry wine and food-led occasions, while Semi-Seco suits dessert, fruit and celebrations where a gentler style is wanted.

Rosé Cava (Rosado)

Rosado Cava is made with authorised red grape varieties, such as Pinot Noir, and can be made in Brut, Extra Brut, Seco and Semi-Seco styles. It is lively, fresh and full of red berry aromas, with a colour that ranges from pale salmon to bright pink. It is a wonderful choice for summer menus, weddings, celebrations and any occasion where a pretty glass matters as much as the taste. Rosé Cava also suits a wider range of food than guests expect, from charcuterie and grilled prawns to sushi and light desserts.

Food Pairing With Cava

Cava’s acidity and bubbles act like a refreshing reset for the palate. They cut through fat, salt and fried textures, and they lift delicate flavours. That is why it works with so many different foods. The poster highlights six reliable matches; for the full theory behind pairing, read our guide to food and wine pairing.

  • Seafood: oysters, prawns, lobster, grilled fish and clams. Brut Nature or Extra Brut is the sharpest match for briny shellfish.
  • Tapas: patatas bravas, jamón ibérico and other Spanish tapas. The bubbles cleanse the palate between rich, spicy and salty bites.
  • Olives: green and black olives. The salty, bitter tang is softened by the wine’s freshness.
  • Cured meats: jamón ibérico, chorizo and salami. Acidity cuts through the fat, and the wine’s toasty notes complement the savoury depth.
  • Fried snacks: calamari, croquetas and padrón peppers. Few wines handle fried food as well as dry sparkling.
  • Soft cheeses: Brie, Camembert, young Manchego and other mild cheeses. The creamy texture is balanced by acidity and bubbles.

As a rule, match the sweetness of the wine to the food. Dry styles suit salty, fried and fatty dishes. Off-dry and Semi-Seco styles suit fruit-based desserts and mildly spiced dishes. Avoid pairing very sweet wine with salty starters, where it can taste cloying.

Famous Cava Cocktails

Cava is an excellent cocktail base because it is dry, crisp and affordable. Four classics from the poster are worth having on every brunch, aperitif and event menu. The proportions below are starting points that you should adapt to your venue’s recipes and glassware.

Cava Mimosa

Cava, fresh orange juice and an orange slice. Light, fresh and refreshing, it is the ultimate brunch drink. Use a flute, pour the juice first, and top gently with chilled Cava, in roughly equal parts or with more Cava for a drier drink.

Cava Royale

Cava, crème de cassis and fresh berries. Elegant and fruity, it follows the style of the classic Kir Royale. Add a small measure of crème de cassis to the glass, top with Cava and finish with a berry.

Cava Spritz

Cava, Aperol, soda water and an orange slice. Bitter-sweet and refreshing, it suits terraces, poolside service and early evenings. Build it over ice in a large wine glass, with the Cava and Aperol first and a splash of soda to finish.

Agua de Valencia

Cava, fresh orange juice, gin, vodka and an orange slice. A classic Valencian cocktail that is strong in disguise, it is usually served in a jug for sharing. Because it combines several spirits, serve it responsibly and make sure guests understand its strength.

For all Cava cocktails, use dry Cava such as Brut, chill every ingredient, squeeze juice fresh, and add the sparkling wine last to keep the bubbles lively.

How to Taste Cava

A short tasting routine helps staff describe Cava with confidence. Look at the colour and the bubbles first: good Cava shows a pale straw to golden colour and a steady stream of fine bubbles rising in the glass. Smell next, noticing citrus, green apple, white flowers and, in longer-aged wines, brioche, almond and toast. Then sip and consider the acidity, which should feel fresh and mouth-watering, the sweetness level, the texture of the bubbles and the length of the finish. Tasting a Brut Nature, a Brut and a Semi-Seco side by side is the fastest way to understand sweetness, and a Reserva next to a young Cava shows what lees ageing adds.

Serving Cava Properly

Temperature

Serve Cava well chilled, at about 6 to 8°C. Too warm, and the bubbles go flat and the wine tastes heavy. Too cold, and the aromas are muted. Chill bottles for several hours in a refrigerator, or for 20 to 30 minutes in an ice bucket filled with ice and water.

Glassware

A flute shows off the bubbles and keeps the wine fizzy, while a tulip-shaped glass concentrates the aromas and suits fuller, longer-aged Cava. Glasses should be spotlessly clean, as grease and detergent residue destroy the bubbles.

Opening the bottle

Open sparkling wine slowly and safely. Remove the foil, loosen the cage while keeping a thumb over the cork, hold the bottle at a 45-degree angle, and twist the bottle, not the cork, while easing the cork out with a gentle sigh rather than a pop. Point the bottle away from guests and never use a knife or force.

Pouring and storage

Pour a small amount first and let the foam settle, then fill to about two thirds. Wrap the bottle in a service cloth to keep it dry and in control. Store unopened bottles on their sides in a cool, dark place, and drink most non-vintage Cava while it is fresh. Once opened, a sparkling-wine stopper will keep the wine lively for a day or two in the refrigerator.

Selling Cava in a Hotel, Restaurant or Bar

Cava gives operators a rare combination of quality, flexibility and margin. These ideas help you get the most from it:

  • Offer it by the glass for aperitifs and brunch, so guests can try it without committing to a bottle.
  • Anchor your brunch menu with Mimosas and Spritzes, and offer bottomless-style packages only where local regulations and responsible service allow.
  • Build a tapas pairing with olives, jamón, croquetas and cheese, and promote a Cava and tapas flight.
  • Use it for toasts and receptions, where its price allows you to serve more guests without compromising on the celebratory feel.
  • Describe it in plain words, such as “crisp, fresh, with citrus and a toasty finish”, and let the guest choose the sweetness.
  • Train the team to explain the difference between Brut Nature, Brut and Semi-Seco, and to open and pour sparkling wine confidently.

Responsible service always applies. Follow your venue’s policies and local laws, keep an eye on the pace of service, offer water, and be prepared for guests who ask about sulphites or other ingredients. If you want a broader vocabulary for explaining wine, our wine terminology guide is a good starting point, and our red wine guide covers the other side of the list.

A Five-Minute Team Briefing on Cava

Before service, brief the team on three points. First, what Cava is: Spanish sparkling wine made in the bottle, mainly in Penedès. Second, how to choose: Brut for most guests, Brut Nature or Extra Brut for very dry lovers, Semi-Seco for dessert and sweeter palates. Third, what to suggest: tapas, seafood and fried snacks for food, and Mimosa, Royale, Spritz and Agua de Valencia for cocktails. A team that can say these three things clearly will sell more Cava and leave guests happier.

Common Cava Mistakes to Avoid

  • Serving Cava too warm or in a dirty or greasy glass.
  • Opening a bottle that has been shaken, or letting the cork fly.
  • Pairing a sweet Cava with salty starters, or a very dry Cava with a sweet dessert.
  • Using a sweet style for cocktails when a dry Brut would be better balanced.
  • Leaving opened bottles at room temperature and serving them flat.
  • Treating Cava as a cheap copy of Champagne instead of a distinct, quality wine in its own right.
  • Overcomplicating the explanation and losing the guest’s interest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cava the same as Champagne?

No. Both are made by the traditional method, but Champagne comes from the Champagne region of France and uses different grapes, while Cava comes mainly from Catalonia and uses Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. The flavours and prices differ as well.

Is Cava the same as Prosecco?

No. Prosecco is Italian, made mainly from the Glera grape and usually by the tank method, which gives lighter, fruitier, more floral wines. Cava is Spanish and made in the bottle, so it is typically crisper, more citrusy and often more toasty.

Which Cava should I choose for a mimosa?

A dry, fresh Brut. It balances the sweetness of the orange juice. Save your finest Gran Reserva for sipping on its own.

How long can an opened bottle of Cava last?

With a proper sparkling-wine stopper and refrigeration, one to two days. After that, the bubbles fade quickly.

Does Cava contain sulphites?

Like most wines, Cava contains sulphites, and this must be declared on the label in many markets. Guests with sensitivities should be encouraged to speak to a manager.

Can Cava age?

Many Cavas are designed to be enjoyed young and fresh, but Reserva and Gran Reserva styles benefit from longer ageing on the lees and can develop beautifully in the bottle.

Final Thoughts

Cava is proof that great sparkling wine does not have to be expensive. It brings together a respected traditional method, distinctive Spanish grapes, a style for every taste from bone dry to gently sweet, and a long list of foods and cocktails that it flatters. For guests, it is an easy yes. For operators, it is a versatile and profitable one.

Use the poster as a quick reference in the training room, at the bar or on the brunch pass, and use this guide for the reasoning behind it. Learn the three grapes, the sweetness levels and the four cocktails, serve it cold and fresh, and always let the guest choose.
